newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechens say they know who shot Red Cross workers.
newsitem.headline: Chechens say they know who shot Red Cross workers.

text.p: The organiser of last month's murder of six foreign Red Cross workers in Chechnya has been identified and is at large somewhere outside the breakaway region, RIA news agency quoted a separatist official as saying.
Abu Movsayev, head of Chechnya's Department of State Security, said the Russian authorities had been asked to help arrest the suspect, who he refused to name, RIA said.

"The identity of the mastermind and organiser of the murder of the doctors on December 17 in Novy Atagi has been established with the maxium exactitude," it quoted him as telling a news conference in the Chechen capital Grozny.
The agency later quoted Russian officials as denying they had received any official request to cooperate in catching a suspect, although they said they were prepared to help if asked.
The six foreign aid workers, five of them women, were gunned down in their beds in a hospital compound in the village of Novy Atagi the most violent incident of its kind in Chechnya.

A Red Cross official in Geneva described the attack as an assassination, while some Chechen separatist leaders said it was "political provocation" aimed at disrupting local presidential and parliamentary elections planned for January 27.
The elections follow a peace deal signed between Moscow and the separatists in August ending 21 months of fighting.

Tim Guldimann, the Swiss diplomat who is trying to broker a lasting settlement, said on Tuesday he was satisfied that last month's flare-up of violence, which included the murder of a group of Russians, had died down.
"There exists a real chance that the elections in Chechnya will be democratic," Interfax news agency quoted him as saying.
Guldimann, who heads the Chechnya mission of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), had expressed concern about the safety of election observers.
He has said a final decision on their deployment will be taken at a session of the Council of Europe on January 16.

Chechen Interior Minister Khasbek Makhashev said on Tuesday he could not exclude "various provocations" during the elections but said special measures would be taken to protect observers and journalists, Itar-Tass news agency reported.

Tens of thousands of people were killed in the conflict between Moscow and the rebels, which began in December 1994 when President Boris Yeltsin sent troops to the region to try to stop moves to split it from the Russian Federation.
Russian officials said on Sunday the last troops had now left the region in line with the peace arrangements.
